passage:
First Tuesday. In the weekly review, Lavanya, the sales head, held up Yogesh's report in front of twelve people. "Did a child write this? Honestly, Yogesh, I expect more from a peon." A few people laughed nervously. Yogesh stared at the table, face burning. That night he couldn't eat. He kept thinking he must be stupid.

The next Monday. It happened again, this time to Meena from accounts. Yogesh watched her eyes fill. Something shifted in him. It wasn't him. It was how Lavanya treated people. He opened a notebook and started writing: dates, exact words, who was present. He asked Meena if she'd do the same.

Three weeks later. With six dated entries and Meena's notes, Yogesh met Mr. Chauhan, a senior director he trusted, and then HR. HR opened a formal review. Yogesh also started walking in the evenings again, and told his sister everything. He was still nervous in meetings. But he no longer believed he deserved it.

qa.q: How many people were in the weekly review when Lavanya mocked Yogesh's report?
qa.a: There were twelve people.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling on the first Tuesday night?
qa.a: Yogesh felt humiliated and ashamed, unable to eat and believing he must be stupid.

qa.q: What steps did Yogesh take to protect himself?
qa.a: He recorded dated incidents with exact words and witnesses, went to a trusted senior and HR, and looked after his health and support.

qa.q: How did Meena seem to experience Lavanya's comments?
qa.a: Meena was hurt and humiliated, her eyes filling with tears in front of everyone.

grounding: The story shows a young man belittled by his manager in meetings who feels humiliated, realises it is not his fault, documents incidents, seeks HR and senior support and protects his health.

passage:
Pradeep, you say your boss mocks you in meetings and you think it's because you're weak. Listen to your Nitin mama.

At twenty-four I worked at a textile firm under a man called Grover. Every Monday he picked someone to tear apart. Often me. "Nitin, your brain is on holiday." "Nitin, go and sell peanuts instead." People laughed so they wouldn't be next. I started getting headaches every Sunday night. I was sure it was my fault.

Then one day I saw him do it to Mrs. Fernandes, who had worked there twenty years and was brilliant. That was my turning point. It wasn't about us. It was him.

I began writing it down in a small diary: date, words, who heard. After two months I took it to Mr. Kulkarni, the senior partner, whom everyone respected. He read it silently, then said, "This stops."

Grover was moved within the year. The headaches stopped sooner, the day I stopped believing him.

qa.q: What did Grover tell Nitin to go and sell?
qa.a: He told him to go and sell peanuts.

qa.q: How did young Nitin feel about Grover's mockery at first?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and anxious, getting headaches every Sunday and believing it was his fault.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nitin's story?
qa.a: Seeing Grover humiliate the brilliant Mrs. Fernandes showed him it wasn't his fault, so he documented incidents and went to a respected senior partner.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Fernandes have felt when Grover mocked her?
qa.a: She was likely humiliated and hurt, even after twenty years of excellent work.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young man belittled by his manager who realised it was not his fault, documented incidents and sought help from a trusted senior.

passage:
At the cooperative dairy office in Anand, Anjali kept the milk collection records. When she pointed out that Rathod sir's new pricing chart underpaid the small farmers, he slammed the register shut. "You're a clerk. Your job is to type, not think. Do it again and I'll see you're transferred to the chilling plant."

The office went silent. Anjali's hands shook for the rest of the day. At home she barely spoke. Maybe she had overstepped.

The next morning Jahnavi, the senior accountant, found her in the storeroom. "I heard. That was a threat, and it's not the first time he's done it. It's not your fault."

"What do I do?"

"Write down exactly what he said and when. I'll write what I saw. Then we both go to the society's chairman, together."

They did, that Friday, with two pages of notes. The chairman asked for the pricing chart to be reviewed, and for Rathod sir to meet him. Anjali also quietly looked at openings in the district office, just to know her options.

qa.a: He threatened to have her transferred to the chilling plant.

qa.a: Anjali felt frightened and shaken, her hands trembling, and wondered if she had overstepped.

qa.q: What steps did Anjali and Jahnavi take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: They recorded what happened, went together to the chairman, and Anjali checked other options, so she was not left alone or silent.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi see Rathod sir's behaviour?
qa.a: Jahnavi sees it as a repeated pattern of threats, and makes sure Anjali knows it is not her fault.

passage:
Nikita, beta, you're afraid to tell your boss she made an error because she gave you your first break. I understand. Let your Parul aunty tell you something.

When I was twenty-five, nobody wanted to hire a woman accountant who'd taken three years off for her father's illness. Mrs. D'Costa did. She said, "I trust you," and she meant it. I would have walked into fire for her.

Six months later, preparing the annual accounts, I found she had booked a large payment in the wrong year. It made the profit look better than it was. I was sick with worry. Who was I to correct her?

The turning point came when I remembered why she'd hired me. "I need someone who will tell me the truth," she'd said in the interview.

So I told her, quietly, with the papers. She read them, took off her glasses and said, "Thank you. That's exactly your job." She fixed it that day. And she trusted me more after.

qa.a: She had taken three years off.

qa.q: How did young Parul feel when she found the wrong entry?
qa.a: She felt grateful to Mrs. D'Costa yet sick with worry about correcting her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Parul's story?

qa.q: How did Mrs. D'Costa see Parul's correction?
qa.a: Mrs. D'Costa valued it, thanking her and saying it was exactly her job, and trusted her more afterwards.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman grateful to a manager who gave her a chance, who stays honest and points out the manager's error, and is valued for it.

passage:
The board presentation was in fifty minutes, the projector in the conference room had just died, and Gurpreet, rechecking the slides on a laptop, saw it: in Nirmala ma'am's summary, the growth figure was eighteen percent. The data said eight.

Gurpreet's stomach dropped. Nirmala had hired Gurpreet when three other managers had said no: "not enough experience". Everything since had come from that one chance. And now, fifty minutes before the board, Gurpreet had to say she was wrong?

The clock ticked. The IT man was still fiddling with the cables.

Gurpreet walked over and spoke quietly. "Ma'am, I think slide four has a typo. The data says eight percent, not eighteen. I'm so grateful for everything you've done for me, and that's why I had to say it."

Nirmala looked, went pale, then laughed shakily. "Eighteen would have been a disaster. Fix it, quickly."

After the meeting she said, "That's why I hired you."

qa.q: What growth figure did the data actually show?
qa.a: The data showed eight percent.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling on seeing the error?
qa.a: Gurpreet's stomach dropped; Gurpreet felt grateful to Nirmala and afraid to correct her so close to the meeting.

qa.q: Why was speaking up the best way for Gurpreet to show gratitude?

qa.q: How did Nirmala respond to Gurpreet's correction?
qa.a: Nirmala was shaken, then relieved and appreciative, saying that was why she had hired Gurpreet.

grounding: The story shows a young employee grateful to a manager who took a chance on them, who stays honest and points out an error, and whose candour is valued.

passage:
Omkar, you talk about your mentor like he's a god. I did that once. Let your Reena aunty tell you how it went.

At twenty-three I joined a newspaper in Pune, and the editor, Mr. Bhonsle, became my hero. His writing was brilliant. I copied his style, his tea, even his way of holding a pen. If he said a story was good, it was good.

Then he killed a story I had worked on for two months, about a factory dumping waste. He said it was "not strong enough". I believed him. Later I found out the factory owner was his friend.

I was so let down I nearly quit journalism.

The turning point was a long talk with an older reporter, Mrs. Shaikh. "He's a fine writer and a flawed man. Take the writing. Keep your own judgment."

After that I still learned from him, but I asked hard questions. And I took the factory story to another paper.

qa.q: What was Reena's killed story about?
qa.a: It was about a factory dumping waste.

qa.q: How did young Reena feel when she found out why the story was killed?
qa.a: She felt deeply let down, disillusioned enough to nearly quit journalism.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Reena's story?

qa.q: How might Mr. Bhonsle have seen Reena's questions afterwards?
qa.a: He may have been surprised or uncomfortable that she no longer accepted everything he said.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young woman who admired her mentor blindly, learned he had flaws, and kept learning from him while asking hard questions and trusting her own judgment.

passage:
It was 2 a.m. on the surgical ward, the lights were flickering in the storm, and Baljeet, a second-year resident, watched Dr. Ganga Menon calm a panicking family in thirty seconds flat. He wanted to be exactly like her. He had copied her handwriting on charts, her way of tying a knot, even her habit of tapping the bed rail twice before speaking.

Then she told him to discharge Mr. Pillai in the morning. Baljeet looked at the numbers. The fever hadn't settled. His stomach tightened. She was never wrong, was she?

He almost said nothing. Then he thought: if I only ever agree, I'm not learning anything.

"Ma'am, can I ask something? His fever hasn't come down. Should we wait a day?"

Dr. Menon looked at the chart for a long moment. "You're right. I was going on yesterday's numbers. Good question."

Baljeet felt something new. Not less admiration. A different kind.

qa.a: It was 2 a.m.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he noticed the fever hadn't settled?
qa.a: Baljeet felt anxious, his stomach tightening, torn between admiration and doubt.

qa.q: Why was asking the question better than silently agreeing?
qa.a: It used his own judgment for the patient's safety, and showed that learning from a mentor includes asking hard questions.

qa.q: How did Dr. Menon react to Baljeet's question?
qa.a: Dr. Menon considered it seriously, admitted her mistake and praised the question.

grounding: The story shows a young doctor who admires his mentor and copies her, who learns to ask a hard question and see her as a person who can be wrong.

Now he had his own small repair shop by the market. The first month's profit was tiny, but it was his.

He wanted to repay her and didn't know how. Money would insult her. So he went to the ITI with a box of bebinca and said, plainly, "Ma'am, everything I know is from you. Thank you."

She smiled and brushed it off. "Show me your shop."

When she came, a nervous boy was sweeping the floor: Rohit, a first-year ITI student. "I'm teaching him on Saturdays," Francis said. "Like you taught me."

Sharmila ma'am looked at the boy for a long moment, then at Francis. Her eyes were wet.

In a bicycle workshop in Barcelona, Kaito had spent three years learning from Pablo, a grey-haired mechanic who explained every spoke and bearing as if it were a poem. Pablo had taken him in when Kaito spoke almost no Spanish, and had never once made him feel slow.

Now Kaito had been offered his own shop in Valencia. On his last evening he stood by the workbench, trying to find the words.

"Pablo, I don't know how to pay you back."

Pablo waved a greasy hand. "Pay me back? Don't be silly."

"Then tell me what you'd want."

Pablo thought. "When some kid comes into your shop who can't speak the language and doesn't know a wrench from a spoon, you teach him. Slowly. That's all."

Kaito nodded, his throat tight. Six months later, in Valencia, a young man from Senegal asked for work. Kaito handed him a wrench and said, "Slowly. We start with the spokes."

passage:
At the research institute, Irfan had admired Dr. Charu Mehta since his first year. She had taught him how to design an experiment, how to write, how to stand his ground at conferences.

Then, on a Thursday, he saw her change three numbers in the shared data sheet so the results looked stronger before the grant deadline. The next week, in the corridor, he heard her mock a junior scientist's accent behind his back.

Irfan felt sick. Was everything she taught him a lie?

He sat in the lab after hours, thinking. No. The method she taught him was real. The writing was real. She was also a person who had just done something wrong.

On Monday he went to her office. "Ma'am, I saw the changes in the data sheet. I can't have my name on the grant report with those numbers." She stiffened. "Fine." He also emailed the lab's research integrity officer, briefly and factually.

He kept her notes on experimental design. They were still the best he had.

qa.a: She changed three numbers.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling after seeing the changes and hearing the mockery?
qa.a: Irfan felt sick and let down, wondering if everything she had taught him was a lie.

qa.q: How did Irfan handle his disillusionment wisely?
qa.a: He kept the lessons that were true, refused to put his name on the altered report, and reported it factually to the integrity officer.

qa.q: How did Dr. Mehta react when Irfan spoke to her?
qa.a: She stiffened and said only "Fine", which suggests she felt caught and defensive.

grounding: The passage shows a young researcher let down when his mentor cuts corners and is petty, who keeps her true lessons and sets a firm boundary on harmful conduct.

Dear Eshaan sir,

Thank you for the two years of guidance. I mean that before anything else. You taught me how to structure a case, how to read a judge, and how to breathe before standing up.

But I have to tell you something honestly. Last Friday, I heard you tell Mr. Rao that Advocate Sheikh was "a nobody who got lucky", and ask him to delay her client's file out of spite. It was small, and it was unfair to her client, who has done nothing wrong.

I was let down. I've looked up to you more than anyone in this profession.

I've thought about it all weekend. I'm not going to pretend it didn't happen, and I'm not going to throw away everything you taught me either. But I won't take part in delaying that file. If I'm asked, I'll say no.

I hope we can still work together. I'm still grateful. I'm just seeing you more clearly.

Parveen

I'm Aparna, the only woman in Pradeep sir's architecture studio, and for eight months I thought I was the lucky one.

He'd picked me as his mentee. "I'll teach you everything," he said. At first he did. Then the "learning" changed. I picked up his dry-cleaning. I booked his daughter's dance classes. I drew the full plans for the hospital wing, and at the client meeting he presented them as his, without my name.

I felt torn. He had opened doors for me. Maybe this was just how it worked? But every evening I went home angry, and I hadn't designed anything of my own in months.

One Monday I said it, as calmly as I could. "Sir, I'm grateful for your guidance. But I want the errands to stop, and I'd like my name on the hospital drawings. I'm here to learn design."

He looked offended. "Ungrateful." Two weeks later, nothing had changed. I applied elsewhere. I start at a new firm in June.

qa.q: What did Aparna pick up for Pradeep sir?
qa.a: She picked up his dry-cleaning.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel about the errands and the lost credit?
qa.a: Aparna felt torn between loyalty and unfairness, going home angry every evening.

qa.q: Why was leaving the right step for Aparna after speaking up?
qa.a: She had spoken up calmly and asked for fair learning and recognition, and when nothing changed, leaving stopped the exploitation.

qa.q: How did Pradeep sir see Aparna's request?
qa.a: Pradeep sir saw it as ingratitude, calling her "Ungrateful" instead of addressing the problem.

grounding: A first-person account shows a young woman whose mentor uses her for errands and takes credit for her work, who speaks up for fair learning and recognition and leaves when nothing changes.

passage:
University career office note, final-year counselling. Student: Eshaan, 23, research intern.

Eshaan came in exhausted. For six months he has worked in Dr. Ankita's lab "for experience": unpaid, weekends included. He showed me a conference paper: his analysis, her name first, his nowhere. He also does her grocery orders and collects her son from school.

He said, "She says this is how everyone learns. Maybe I'm being ungrateful." Then, more quietly, "But I haven't learned anything new since March."

I told him that feeling pulled between gratitude and a sense of unfairness is common in these situations, and that it is reasonable to expect real teaching and credit.

We planned a short conversation: thank her for the opportunity, ask for his name on the paper, ask to stop personal errands, and ask for one new skill to learn this term. If nothing changes in a month, we will look at other labs together.

Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: For how long has Eshaan worked in Dr. Ankita's lab?
qa.a: He has worked there for six months.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about his work in the lab?
qa.a: Eshaan felt exhausted and torn, worrying he was ungrateful while feeling it was unfair.

In the small town of Aldona in Goa, Nazia had learned everything about baking from Maria aunty: how to feel when dough was ready, how to fold butter for puffs. For three years she worked in Maria's bakery at dawn.

Then Nazia started making cakes on her own for weddings, and people began asking for her by name. Maria aunty grew quiet. She told a customer that Nazia's cakes "look nice but taste of nothing". She stopped lending her the big oven.

passage:
Monday, late.

Gopika, the new intern, asked me today how I got so good at client pitches. She said, "Everyone says you're the best, sir." I felt about ten feet tall. I told her a long story about the Sharma account that made me sound like a genius. I left out the part where I nearly lost it.

On the drive home I felt a bit embarrassed. I'd enjoyed being looked up to a little too much. Was I helping her, or just polishing my own reflection?

So tomorrow, I'll tell her the real Sharma story: I misread the brief, the client almost walked out, and my boss saved me. That's where I actually learned.

And I'll stop answering every question for her. Next time she asks how to structure a deck, I'll ask, "How would you do it?" first.

I'm Lalit, and I'm not her hero. I'm her guide for a while. That's better.

qa.q: What did Gopika ask Lalit about?
qa.a: She asked how he got so good at client pitches.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel on the drive home?
qa.a: Lalit felt a bit embarrassed, aware of enjoying being looked up to too much.

qa.q: What will Lalit change in how he mentors Gopika?
qa.a: He'll share his real failure on the Sharma account and ask her how she'd do things first, to encourage her independence.

qa.q: How might Gopika benefit from hearing the real Sharma story?
qa.a: Gopika may feel less intimidated and learn that mistakes are part of growing, not a sign of failure.

grounding: A diary entry shows a young man who feels proud and self-important when an intern looks up to him, who decides to share his failures and encourage her independence.

passage:
Bidisha had until Friday at five to accept the job in Bengaluru, and it was already Thursday night. Her old mentor, Vidya ma'am, who had taught her everything about accounting at the firm in Kolkata, had called that afternoon. "Stay in audit. Startups are unstable. Trust me, I've seen it."

For five years Bidisha had followed that voice. Tonight it felt too small. She had studied the startup's numbers, met the founders twice, and knew what she wanted: to build a finance team from scratch.

She felt disloyal just thinking it.

At ten she called back. "Ma'am, everything I know about reading a balance sheet is from you. That's why I've gone through this company's books properly. I'm going to take it. I know you worry, and I'm grateful you care."

There was a long pause. Then Vidya laughed softly. "Your first independent decision. Good. Send me the balance sheet anyway."

qa.q: By when did Bidisha have to accept the job?
qa.a: She had until Friday at five.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling about disagreeing with Vidya ma'am?
qa.a: Bidisha felt disloyal and torn, even though she knew what she wanted.

qa.q: How did Bidisha disagree respectfully?
qa.a: She thanked Vidya ma'am for what she taught, explained she had checked the company carefully using those lessons, and stated her choice clearly.

qa.q: How did Vidya ma'am take being outgrown?
qa.a: Vidya ma'am was glad, laughing softly and calling it Bidisha's first independent decision.

grounding: The story shows a young woman who has outgrown her mentor's advice and feels disloyal for disagreeing, who honours her, disagrees respectfully and finds her mentor glad.

passage:
Darshan sir had taught Yogesh to cook in the busy kitchen of a Bandra restaurant: knife skills, timing, how to take criticism without crying in the cold room. For four years, Yogesh never questioned a single recipe.

Now Yogesh ran the kitchen of his own small café in Mahim, and Darshan sir came to eat. Afterwards he said, "Too much experimenting. Stick to the classics. People want butter chicken, not millet risotto."

Yogesh felt his face go warm. The millet dishes were selling out every day. But arguing felt like betrayal.

He sat down across from his old teacher. "Sir, everything in this kitchen stands on what you taught me. The timing, the knife work, even how I talk to my staff. But I think the millet dishes are right for this place. They're our best sellers."

Darshan sir was silent. Then he pointed his fork at the risotto. "Too much salt," he said. And then, almost smiling, "But the idea is good."

qa.q: Where was Yogesh's own café?
qa.a: His café was in Mahim.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when Darshan sir criticised the menu?
qa.a: Yogesh felt his face go warm, torn and feeling disloyal for wanting to disagree.

qa.q: How did Yogesh disagree with his mentor respectfully?
qa.a: He first honoured what Darshan sir taught him, then calmly explained why the millet dishes suited his café, backed by what was selling.

qa.q: How might Darshan sir have felt hearing Yogesh disagree?
qa.a: Darshan sir seemed quietly proud, still giving honest feedback on the salt but admitting the idea was good.

grounding: The passage shows a young chef who has grown beyond his mentor's advice and feels disloyal, who honours what his mentor gave and respectfully says where he differs.
